election observer — The role involves observing voting procedures independently and assessing how the election was conducted.
vote counting — This process turns the marked ballots into numerical election results.
voter turnout — It is the share of eligible people who actually cast a ballot.
invalid ballot — A voting paper that cannot be accepted under the rules is left out of the result.
right to privacy — It protects information about a person's private life against unjustified intrusion or disclosure.
freedom of movement — It covers travelling within a country and choosing one's place of residence.
non-discrimination — The principle forbids unfair treatment based only on protected personal characteristics.
right to a fair trial — It requires an independent hearing in which the accused can present a defence.

World Economic Forum — The World Economic Forum is known for its annual Davos meeting of political and business leaders.
Europol — This agency supports cooperation and information sharing among European law-enforcement authorities.
G7 — It is an informal group of seven major advanced democracies whose leaders meet annually.
European Council — It brings together national leaders and defines the European Union's broad priorities.
Frontex — The agency coordinates European cooperation in managing external borders.
ambassador — This official is a country's highest-ranking diplomatic representative abroad.
diplomatic immunity — It gives accredited envoys defined protections from the host state's legal jurisdiction.
diplomatic bag — This protected package carries official communications between a mission and its government.
state visit — A state visit is a formal visit by one head of state to another country at that country's head-of-state invitation, with the highest level of ceremonial welcome.
bilateral agreement — It is a formal deal made between two countries or other parties.
payslip — The document itemises a worker's earnings and deductions for a payment date.
gross pay — This is the worker's total amount before deductions are removed.
net pay — This is the amount the worker actually receives after deductions.

pay period — It is the span of time covered by one wage payment.
discount — It is a reduction from the normal amount charged for a product or service.
price comparison website — The site gathers offers so shoppers can compare prices across different sellers.
unit price — It expresses a product's cost for one standard quantity, such as a kilogram or litre.
interest rate — This percentage determines interest charged on a loan or paid on savings.
consumer price index — It follows how the prices paid for a representative shopping basket change over time.
job interview — It lets an employer assess a candidate and lets the candidate learn about the role.
employment contract — The agreement establishes the terms under which a person works for an employer.
timesheet — It records the duration an employee spent on each task.
probationary period — This initial employment interval allows both employer and employee to assess whether the arrangement works.

assertion: notice period — It is the time that runs from notification of termination until the final day of work.
currency symbol — It is a compact sign used to show which money unit an amount uses.
banknote serial number — Bank of England notes use this letter-and-number combination as a unique identifier for each individual note.

supportingSource.title: Bank of England Museum: Plates and dies

assertion: banknote watermark — The image is formed within the paper and can be checked against transmitted light.
commemorative coin — Eesti Pank distinguishes circulating two-euro commemorative coins with special designs marking important national or European events from collector coins.
security thread — The embedded strip is one of the features used to authenticate paper money.
Swiss franc — This is the official money of both Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Swedish krona — Sweden uses this national money instead of the euro.
Danish krone — Denmark uses this national money instead of the euro.
Polish złoty — Its name is connected to the Polish adjective for golden.
Hungarian forint — Hungary uses this national money instead of the euro.
witness stand — It is the designated place in a courtroom from which a witness gives testimony.
court interpreter — The role allows participants who use different languages to understand spoken proceedings.

supportingSource.title: Utah State Courts: How to Become a Court Interpreter

assertion: plaintiff — This is the party that initiates a civil case against another party.
court clerk — This official handles administrative records and documents for the judicial process.
courtroom sketch artist — This person draws scenes from proceedings that cannot be freely photographed or filmed.
arrest warrant — An arrest warrant is a court-issued document authorising the arrest and detention of a specified person.
search warrant — A search warrant authorises police to search a specified place for evidence of a crime.
case file — A case file is the collection of procedural documents and other relevant information kept for one court case.

supportingSource.title: Estonian Code of Civil Procedure: Chapter 9, Case File

assertion: power of attorney — A power of attorney lets one person act on another person's behalf in specified matters.
restraining order — A restraining order directs a person to keep away from and avoid contacting another person.
speed limit — A speed limit sets the highest legal driving speed for a stretch of road.
speed camera — A speed camera records vehicles that exceed the legal maximum speed.
breathalyser — A breathalyser estimates alcohol in a person's body by analysing a breath sample.
parking ticket — A parking ticket is a penalty notice issued for leaving a vehicle where or when it is not allowed.
vehicle inspection — A vehicle inspection is a periodic official check of a vehicle's roadworthiness.
food bank — A food bank collects and distributes donated groceries to people in need.
neighbourhood watch — Neighbourhood watch involves residents cooperating and reporting suspicious local activity to help prevent crime.
blood donation — Blood donation is the voluntary giving of blood for use in treating patients.
community garden — A community garden is a shared plot cultivated by local residents.
charity shop — A charity shop sells donated goods and uses the proceeds to support a cause.
first impression — A first impression is an initial opinion formed when one person first encounters another.
social norm — A social norm is an unwritten rule describing behaviour that a group generally expects.
culture shock — Culture shock is confusion or discomfort caused by entering an unfamiliar culture or way of life.
generation gap — A generation gap is a difference in attitudes or habits between younger and older generations.
bystander effect — The bystander effect makes an individual less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present.
campaign rally — A campaign rally is a public election event where a candidate speaks to a gathering of supporters.

supportingSource.title: University of Delaware Library: Campaign events — Trail to the Voting Booth

assertion: opinion poll — An opinion poll surveys a selected group to measure what people think about a subject.
letter to the editor — A letter to the editor is a reader's message submitted to a publication for its comment section.
letter-writing campaign — A letter-writing campaign organises many people to write to a decision-maker in support of the same change.

supportingSource.title: Resource Centre: Organising a letter-writing campaign

assertion: public consultation — A public consultation invites residents and organisations to comment before an authority makes a decision.
school bell — A school bell signals when a lesson or another part of the school day begins or ends.
school lunch — A school lunch is a midday meal served to pupils during the school day.
school uniform — A school uniform is matching clothing that pupils at an institution are required to wear.
pencil case — It is a small container for writing tools such as pens and pencils.
class trip — A class trip takes pupils away from their usual classroom for an organised educational visit.
lecture hall — A lecture hall is a large room with rows of seats for talks at a university.
student ID card — A student ID card proves enrolment and can provide access to services and resources on campus.
student union — A student union represents students at a college or university and often provides services for them.
university library — A university library provides books, journals, databases, and other resources for higher education and research.
thesis defence — A thesis defence is a formal session in which a student presents research and answers examiners' questions.
online course — An online course provides its lessons and learning activities through the internet.

adult education — Adult education is education and organised learning for adults, including finishing school, basic literacy, and learning new skills.
apprenticeship — An apprenticeship combines practical workplace training with organised study.

median age — The median age divides a population into two equal-sized groups, one younger and one older.
population pyramid — A population pyramid uses opposing bars to show the age and sex distribution of a population.
sex ratio — The sex ratio compares the number of males with the number of females in a population.
baby boom — A baby boom is a temporary period with a sharp rise in the number of births.
ageing population — An ageing population has a growing proportion of older people.

assertion: population decline — Population decline means that the total number of residents falls over time.
return migration — Return migration is the movement of people back to their country of origin after they have lived abroad.
brain drain — Brain drain is the departure of highly trained or qualified people to work or settle elsewhere.
exit poll — An exit poll surveys voters immediately after they leave the polling station, giving broadcasters an early basis for projecting the result.
election ink — Election ink leaves a hard-to-remove mark on a voter, helping election officials prevent the same person from voting twice.
hanging chad — A hanging chad is a punched-card fragment that remains attached by one corner, a disputed ballot feature made famous by Florida in 2000.
Swingometer — The BBC Swingometer turned changes in party support into a visual indication of the parliamentary seats likely to change hands.
Dewey Defeats Truman — The Chicago Daily Tribune printed “Dewey Defeats Truman” too early; the victorious Truman was later photographed holding the mistaken front page.
Watergate scandal — Watergate grew from the Democratic headquarters break-in and its cover-up into the scandal that ended Richard Nixon’s presidency.
Panama Papers — The Panama Papers were leaked Mossack Fonseca files that revealed offshore companies and their owners across the world.
Cambridge Analytica data scandal — The Cambridge Analytica scandal concerned Facebook-app data passed to a political consultancy and used for voter profiling without informed consent.
Iran–Contra affair — In the Iran–Contra affair, secret arms sales to Iran helped finance Nicaragua’s Contras despite restrictions imposed by Congress.
Teapot Dome scandal — Teapot Rock gave its name to the Wyoming oil field whose secret leasing and bribes became the Harding-era Teapot Dome scandal.
Orange Revolution — Viktor Yushchenko’s campaign colour became the emblem and name of Ukraine’s Orange Revolution after the disputed presidential runoff.
Rose Revolution — Georgia’s Rose Revolution took its flower name from demonstrators who entered parliament carrying roses before Eduard Shevardnadze resigned.
Saffron Revolution — Myanmar’s Saffron Revolution was named for the robe colour associated with the Buddhist monks who led the protests.
Cedar Revolution — Lebanon’s Cedar Revolution invoked the cedar displayed on the national flag during protests demanding Syrian troop withdrawal.
Jasmine Revolution — Jasmine, Tunisia’s national flower and a bloom prized for fragrance and perfume, supplied a Western nickname for the country’s 2011 revolution.
Tank Man — Tank Man is the nickname for the unidentified shopper who stood in front of a tank column in Beijing after the 1989 crackdown.
yellow vests protests — France’s yellow vests movement adopted the high-visibility road-safety vest as the symbol of protests over fuel taxes and living costs.
Umbrella Movement — The Umbrella Movement took its name from the umbrellas Hong Kong demonstrators used as shields against pepper spray.
Extinction Rebellion — Extinction Rebellion is a climate movement associated with nonviolent civil disobedience and an hourglass symbol inside a circle.
Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo — The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo wore white headscarves while demanding answers about children who disappeared under Argentina’s dictatorship.

supportingSource.title: Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo

assertion: Ice Bucket Challenge — The Ice Bucket Challenge spread through nomination videos in which participants doused themselves with ice water and raised funds and awareness for ALS.
Movember — Movember blends moustache with November: participants grow moustaches during the month to support men’s-health fundraising.
Earth Hour — Earth Hour is a WWF-backed action in which non-essential lights are switched off for one evening hour.
Red Nose Day — Red Nose Day is Comic Relief’s recurring UK fundraising event, recognized by its foam clown noses and television appeal.
Livestrong wristband — The yellow silicone Livestrong wristband became a major 2000s cancer-fundraising symbol associated with Lance Armstrong’s foundation.
shrinkflation — Shrinkflation means reducing a package’s quantity while leaving its displayed price unchanged or nearly unchanged.
Big Mac Index — The Economist’s Big Mac Index compares the same burger’s price across currencies as an informal measure of purchasing power.
planned obsolescence — The Phoebus cartel’s reduction of light-bulb life is often cited as a historical example of planned obsolescence.
razor-and-blades model — The razor-and-blades model pairs a cheap initial product, such as a printer, with profitable recurring consumables such as ink cartridges.
lipstick effect — The lipstick effect is the proposed tendency for consumers to keep buying small affordable luxuries during difficult economic periods.
dot-com bubble — The dot-com bubble was the late-1990s surge in internet-company investment and valuations followed by a broad collapse.
tulip mania — Tulip mania describes the Dutch Golden Age boom and collapse in prices for contracts tied to fashionable tulip bulbs.
GameStop short squeeze — The GameStop short squeeze saw Reddit-organized retail buying drive up the retailer’s shares and force short sellers to cover.
Black Wednesday — On Black Wednesday, Britain stopped defending sterling inside the European Exchange Rate Mechanism and withdrew the pound from it.
South Sea Bubble — The South Sea Bubble was the 1720 boom and collapse in shares of Britain’s South Sea Company amid trade and debt-conversion promises.
Theranos — Theranos claimed that tiny blood samples could support many tests, but its technology and claims collapsed into a fraud scandal.
Lehman Brothers — Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy in 2008, and its collapse played a major role as the financial crisis unfolded.
Enron — Enron used deceptive accounting to hide debt and inflate profits before the energy trader entered bankruptcy.
Wirecard — Wirecard failed after auditors could not verify €1.9 billion supposedly held for the German payments company.
Barings Bank — Barings Bank collapsed after Nick Leeson concealed unauthorized derivatives trades made in Singapore.
cocoa beans — Cocoa beans, later processed into chocolate, also circulated as a means of payment in Mesoamerica.
tea bricks — Tea bricks were compressed blocks valued for durability and portability and used as currency along Asian trade routes.
tally sticks — Tally sticks recorded obligations with notches; splitting a stick created matching halves that could later be compared.
cowrie shells — Cowrie shells are glossy sea-snail shells that served as money for centuries across parts of Africa and Asia.
rai stones — Rai stones are Yap’s carved limestone discs; ownership could be transferred publicly without physically moving the stone.
four-day workweek — Perpetual Guardian’s four-day-workweek trial gave staff one nominated weekday off at full pay and was later adopted permanently.
universal basic income — Finland’s universal-basic-income trial paid selected unemployed people regularly without requiring them to seek or accept work.
London congestion charge — The London congestion charge requires most drivers to pay for entering the central charging zone during operating hours.
Gross National Happiness — Gross National Happiness is Bhutan’s well-being-centred development framework, promoted as an alternative to judging progress by GDP alone.
Alaska Permanent Fund dividend — The Alaska Permanent Fund invests a share of oil revenue and pays an annual dividend to eligible Alaska residents.
Left-Handed Whopper — Burger King’s April Fool advertisement described a Left-Handed Whopper with its condiments rotated 180 degrees for southpaw customers.
spaghetti-tree hoax — The BBC’s spaghetti-tree hoax showed a Swiss family harvesting strands from branches in a Panorama April Fool report.
Balloon Boy — The Balloon Boy story followed a helium balloon thought to carry Falcon Heene, although the child was later found hiding at home.
Hitler Diaries — The Hitler Diaries published by Stern were exposed as forgeries made by Konrad Kujau rather than the dictator’s private journals.
Great Moon Hoax — The Great Moon Hoax was a New York Sun series claiming that John Herschel’s telescope had revealed fantastic creatures on the Moon.
Moscow–Washington hotline — The Moscow–Washington hotline began operating in 1963 so the two governments could communicate directly in a crisis; its first generation carried written messages.
shuttle diplomacy — Shuttle diplomacy has a mediator move repeatedly between parties; Kissinger's 1970s Middle East trips made the expression famous.
gunboat diplomacy — Gunboat diplomacy means pursuing foreign-policy aims through conspicuous displays or threats of naval power.
Kitchen Debate — The Kitchen Debate was an improvised public exchange between Nixon and Khrushchev in the model kitchen at the American National Exhibition in Moscow.
cricket diplomacy — Cricket diplomacy describes using the sport and high-profile India–Pakistan matches to help improve relations between the two countries.
Obama Hope poster — The Obama Hope poster was Fairey's widely reproduced 2008 campaign image, built around Obama's stylized portrait and the word “HOPE.”
We Can Do It! poster — “We Can Do It!” was J. Howard Miller's wartime Westinghouse poster; its later reuse linked the image strongly with Rosie the Riveter.
Daisy advertisement — The Daisy advertisement, also called “Peace, Little Girl,” used the nuclear sequence to frame the stakes of the Johnson–Goldwater election.
Morning in America — “Morning in America,” formally “Prouder, Stronger, Better,” was Reagan's 1984 television ad built from upbeat scenes of everyday life.
Labour Isn't Working — “Labour Isn't Working” paired the wordplay with a staged queue outside an unemployment office and became an emblem of the Conservative campaign.
Tahrir Square — Tahrir Square is the major public square in central Cairo that became the focal point of the 2011 uprising against Hosni Mubarak.
Maidan Nezalezhnosti — Maidan Nezalezhnosti means Independence Square; the central Kyiv plaza was the principal site of the Euromaidan demonstrations.
Taksim Square — Taksim Square is a central Istanbul public space containing the Republic Monument and adjoining Gezi Park, the starting point of the 2013 protests.
Azadi Square — Azadi Square surrounds Azadi Tower in Tehran; it was formerly Shahyad Square and was renamed after the Iranian Revolution.
Pearl Roundabout — Pearl Roundabout was a Manama traffic circle and monument whose six sails supported a pearl; it became a protest focus and was demolished in March 2011.
red tape — Red tape is a metaphor for burdensome bureaucracy, associated with the historical practice of binding official documents in red ribbon.
soapbox — A soapbox was literally a sturdy crate for shipping soap; speakers used such boxes as raised platforms, creating the modern political metaphor.
gerrymandering — Gerrymandering is manipulating electoral-district boundaries for political advantage; the term combined Gerry's name with the salamander-shaped district cartoon.
filibuster — A filibuster is a parliamentary delaying tactic, often a prolonged speech; its word history runs through terms meaning freebooter or pirate.
pork barrel politics — Pork barrel politics is public spending targeted at a representative's district, named through the image of a barrel that stored and distributed salted pork.
Zimbabwean dollar — The Zimbabwean dollar suffered extreme hyperinflation and its final series included a 100-trillion-dollar note; it was suspended in 2009.
Greek capital controls — Greek capital controls were imposed in 2015, closing banks temporarily and limiting ATM cash withdrawals during the debt and bailout confrontation.
Tequila crisis — The Tequila crisis was the 1994–95 Mexican peso crisis, when devaluation and lost investor confidence led to an international financial rescue.
Northern Rock bank run — The Northern Rock bank run began after news of emergency central-bank support became public, producing conspicuous queues of depositors outside branches.
corralito — The corralito was Argentina's restriction on bank withdrawals during the 2001 crisis; its nickname literally evokes a small enclosure.
Rana Plaza collapse — The Rana Plaza collapse killed more than 1,100 people in 2013 and focused global attention on conditions in Bangladesh's export-garment industry.
Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire — The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire killed 146 garment workers and helped spur major factory-safety and labour reforms in New York.
Ford's five-dollar day — Ford's five-dollar day raised eligible workers' daily compensation to five dollars and helped the company retain labour for mass production.
Matchgirls' strike — The Matchgirls' strike was a successful walkout by women and teenage girls at Bryant & May's London match factory over pay deductions and working conditions.
Flint sit-down strike — In the Flint sit-down strike of 1936–37, workers stayed inside GM factories; the settlement recognized the United Auto Workers as bargaining representative.
bus rapid transit — Bus rapid transit gives buses faster, higher-capacity service through features such as dedicated lanes and off-board payment; Curitiba became its best-known early model.
Vélib' — Vélib' is Paris's public bicycle-sharing system; its name contracts “vélo” and “liberté.”
Ciclovía — Bogotá's Ciclovía turns more than 100 kilometres of roads into car-free public space on Sundays and holidays.
Strøget — Strøget is Copenhagen's central pedestrian shopping street; its 1962 conversion became an influential early example of large-scale pedestrianisation.
Gemeindebau — A Gemeindebau is municipal housing in Vienna; the celebrated programme expanded greatly under the Social Democratic city government between the world wars.
New Coke — New Coke was Coca-Cola's 1985 reformulation; hostile public reaction led the company to return the original formula as Coca-Cola Classic.

Fairtrade certification — The Fairtrade mark identifies products certified under Fairtrade standards intended to support producers and more equitable trading conditions.
Energy Star — Energy Star is a voluntary programme created by the US EPA to identify products and buildings meeting energy-efficiency criteria.
Nordic Swan Ecolabel — The Nordic Swan Ecolabel is the Nordic countries' official environmental certification scheme, represented by a stylized swan.
FSC certification — FSC certification uses a tree-and-check logo to identify forest products covered by the council's responsible forest-management and chain-of-custody standards.
marshmallow test — The marshmallow test studied delayed gratification by asking young children to choose between one immediate reward and a larger delayed reward.
Asch conformity experiments — The Asch conformity experiments tested whether people would repeat a group's incorrect line-length judgment despite clear visual evidence.
Milgram experiment — Stanley Milgram's experiment tested obedience to authority by making participants believe they were administering increasingly severe electric shocks.
Third Wave experiment — The Third Wave was Ron Jones's 1967 classroom experiment, an authoritarian movement devised while teaching how Germans could have accepted Nazism.
Robbers Cave experiment — The Robbers Cave experiment studied intergroup conflict by creating competition between two groups of boys and then introducing shared, superordinate goals.
panda diplomacy — Panda diplomacy is China's use of giant-panda gifts and, more recently, loans as diplomatic gestures toward other countries.
Resolute desk — The Resolute desk was made from HMS Resolute timbers and presented by Queen Victoria to President Rutherford B. Hayes in 1880; many later presidents used it in the Oval Office.
Washington's Japanese cherry trees — Washington's Japanese cherry trees came from a 1912 gift by Tokyo to symbolize friendship; their bloom is celebrated by the National Cherry Blossom Festival.
Trafalgar Square Christmas tree — The Trafalgar Square Christmas tree is Norway's annual gift to London, given since 1947 in gratitude for British support during the war.

Canadian Tulip Festival — The Canadian Tulip Festival grew from Dutch gifts thanking Canada for sheltering the royal family and for its role in the Netherlands' liberation during the Second World War.
Bernie Sanders inauguration mittens — Bernie Sanders’ inauguration mittens became a viral image after he wore them at the 2021 ceremony; a Vermont teacher made them from repurposed sweaters.
Gandhi's charkha — Gandhi’s charkha, or spinning wheel, symbolised swadeshi self-reliance and appeared on an early version of India’s national flag.
Thatcher's handbag — Margaret Thatcher’s handbag became such a familiar symbol of her authority that “handbagging” came to mean subjecting someone to forceful treatment.
Mao suit — The Mao suit is the Western name for the Zhongshan suit, strongly associated with Mao Zedong and later Chinese leaders.
Tito's Blue Train — Tito’s Blue Train served Josip Broz Tito for state travel and transported many visiting leaders during Yugoslavia’s non-aligned era.
Pirate Party — The Pirate Party movement began in Sweden in 2006 and spread internationally with programmes centred on information policy and digital rights.
Official Monster Raving Loony Party — The Official Monster Raving Loony Party is a British satirical party founded by Screaming Lord Sutch in 1982.
Polish Beer-Lovers' Party — The Polish Beer-Lovers’ Party promoted beer-drinking culture and won sixteen seats in Poland’s 1991 parliamentary election.
Best Party — Iceland’s Best Party was founded by Jón Gnarr and became the largest party on Reykjavík City Council in 2010.
Rhinoceros Party — Canada’s Rhinoceros Party made absurd campaign promises and treated Cornelius the rhinoceros as its symbolic leader.
Boaty McBoatface — Boaty McBoatface topped the public poll; the ship became RRS Sir David Attenborough while an onboard submersible received the winning name.
Moo Deng — Moo Deng is a pygmy hippo at Thailand’s Khao Kheow Open Zoo whose public-poll name translates as “bouncy pork” or “bouncy pig”.
Trainy McTrainface — Trainy McTrainface won MTR Express’s public poll and was assigned to one of its Swedish trains.
Mister Splashy Pants — Mister Splashy Pants won Greenpeace’s whale-naming poll after an online campaign greatly increased participation.
Vinicius and Tom — Vinicius and Tom won Rio 2016’s public mascot-name vote, honouring lyricist Vinicius de Moraes and composer Tom Jobim, who co-wrote “The Girl from Ipanema”.
2020 vice-presidential debate fly — The fly on Mike Pence’s head became one of the most discussed images from the 2020 vice-presidential debate.
Dean scream — The Dean scream was Howard Dean’s emphatic yell after the 2004 Iowa caucuses; repeated broadcasts made it a campaign-defining clip.
Dukakis tank photograph — The Dukakis tank photograph came from a campaign stop intended to project military credibility but became a lasting symbol of the failed campaign.
Four Seasons Total Landscaping press conference — The Four Seasons Total Landscaping press conference became famous for its unexpected industrial-estate setting beside the company’s garage door.

assertion: Checkers speech — The Checkers speech took its name from the Nixon family dog mentioned during the televised defence of Nixon’s finances.
“Greed is good” line — The “greed is good” line is Gordon Gekko’s signature claim in Wall Street and was adapted from a real remark by financier Ivan Boesky.
Springfield monorail — Springfield’s monorail is sold by Lyle Lanley after the town receives a large fine from Mr. Burns; the train proves dangerously defective on its first run.
Fidelity Fiduciary Bank run — The Fidelity Fiduciary Bank run begins when Michael Banks asks for his money and customers mistakenly fear that the bank cannot repay deposits.
Trading Places orange-juice futures — Trading Places ends with the heroes profiting from frozen concentrated orange-juice futures after exposing the villains’ stolen crop report.
Underpants Gnomes business plan — The Underpants Gnomes business plan satirises schemes that jump from an activity to profit without explaining the crucial middle step.
daylight saving time — Daylight saving time advances clocks for part of the year so that evening daylight lasts later by the clock.
seat-belt legislation — Seat-belt legislation requires vehicle occupants to use installed restraints; adoption spread internationally during the late twentieth century.
container-deposit system — A container-deposit system attaches a refundable deposit to drink packaging to encourage collection and recycling.
plastic-bag charge — A plastic-bag charge or levy makes shoppers pay for disposable bags and is used to reduce their consumption and litter.
Dagen H — Dagen H, or H day, was 3 September 1967, when Sweden changed from left-hand to right-hand traffic.
2020 toilet-paper shortage — The 2020 toilet-paper shortage was driven largely by sudden stockpiling and a mismatch between household and commercial supply chains rather than a lack of raw material.

supportingSource.title: Shortages related to the COVID-19 pandemic

assertion: PlayStation 5 shortage — The PlayStation 5 shortage followed the console’s 2020 launch as semiconductor constraints and exceptionally high demand limited availability.
1973 oil crisis — The 1973 oil crisis followed an OAPEC embargo during the Yom Kippur War and caused sharp price rises and fuel shortages in importing countries.
Tickle Me Elmo shortage — Tickle Me Elmo became the 1996 holiday season’s hardest-to-find toy after unexpected demand overwhelmed available supplies.
Cabbage Patch Kids shopping riots — The Cabbage Patch Kids craze peaked during the 1983 holiday season, when limited supplies of the adoptable dolls prompted chaotic scenes among shoppers.
reverse-vending machine — A reverse-vending machine accepts used drink containers and returns a deposit or reward after identifying and sorting them.
repair café — A Repair Café is a free meeting place where visitors repair household items with tools and help from knowledgeable volunteers.
right to repair — The right to repair seeks to let consumers and independent technicians obtain the information, parts, and tools needed to fix products.
Library of Things — A Library of Things lends useful objects that people need only occasionally, reducing the need for every household to buy its own.
pay as you throw — Pay as you throw charges households according to the amount of non-recycled waste they present for collection.
Pet Rock — Pet Rock creator Gary Dahl packaged stones as joke pets; the fad sold more than a million units in the mid-1970s.
fidget-spinner craze — The fidget-spinner craze exploded in 2017; retailers reported high sales, while classroom disruption led some schools to ban the toys.
Beanie Babies bubble — The Beanie Babies bubble grew from collecting and speculation in Ty plush toys, then burst around the end of the 1990s.
Pogs craze — The Pogs craze revived the milk-caps game: players used a slammer to flip stacks of collectible cardboard discs.
Gogo's Crazy Bones craze — Gogo’s Crazy Bones were collectible plastic playing pieces used in several playground games and traded in waves of popularity.
White House — The White House is the US president’s official residence and workplace at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C.
10 Downing Street — 10 Downing Street in Westminster is the official residence and executive office of the United Kingdom’s prime minister.
Élysée Palace — The Élysée Palace is the official residence of the president of France and the site of the presidential office.
Casa Rosada — The Casa Rosada is the Argentine president’s official workplace in Buenos Aires; its name means “the pink house” and its characteristic colour is baby pink.
Palace of Moncloa — The Palace of Moncloa is the official residence and principal workplace of Spain’s prime minister.
George H. W. Bush vomiting incident — The George H. W. Bush vomiting incident occurred at a Tokyo banquet after the president became acutely ill during a tour of Asia.

supportingSource.title: George H. W. Bush vomiting incident

assertion: shoe-banging incident — The shoe-banging incident refers to Khrushchev’s outburst at the UN General Assembly; accounts and photographs leave the exact desk-banging claim disputed.
Russian reset — The US–Russia reset button symbolised an attempted fresh start, but the Russian word printed on it was mistranslated.
Sofagate — Sofagate was the controversy over seating Ursula von der Leyen apart from Charles Michel and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan during an Ankara meeting.
Shamrock Summit — The Shamrock Summit was the 1985 Reagan–Mulroney meeting in Quebec City, remembered for the leaders’ conspicuous Irish-themed friendship.
Oslo Accords — The Oslo Accords grew from secret Norway talks between Israel and the PLO and produced the famous 1993 White House handshake.
Helsinki Accords — The 1975 Helsinki Accords concluded the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe and grouped commitments on security, cooperation, and human rights.
Dayton Agreement — The Dayton Agreement was initialled near Dayton, Ohio, in 1995 and formally signed in Paris, ending the Bosnian War.
Plaza Accord — The 1985 Plaza Accord joined France, West Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States in coordinated action to depreciate the dollar.
Algiers Accords — The 1981 Algiers Accords ended the Iran hostage crisis, arranged the hostages’ release, and established the Iran–United States Claims Tribunal.
Tear Down This Wall speech — Reagan’s 1987 Berlin address became famous for his challenge to Gorbachev concerning the Berlin Wall.
Ich bin ein Berliner speech — Kennedy delivered the Ich bin ein Berliner speech outside Rathaus Schöneberg in 1963 as a declaration of US solidarity with West Berlin.
Blood, Toil, Tears and Sweat speech — Churchill delivered Blood, Toil, Tears and Sweat on 13 May 1940 after forming a wartime coalition government.
Rivers of Blood speech — The Rivers of Blood speech was Powell’s controversial 1968 address opposing Commonwealth immigration; its familiar title came from his classical quotation.
Tryst with Destiny speech — Nehru’s Tryst with Destiny speech marked India’s independence and was delivered to the Constituent Assembly on the eve of 15 August 1947.
Buy Nothing Day — Buy Nothing Day asks participants to make no purchases for a day and uses the Black Friday shopping rush to question overconsumption.
Nestlé boycott — The Nestlé boycott began in 1977 over the company’s marketing of infant formula in developing countries and continued through later monitoring and relaunches.
Icelandic Women’s Day Off — Iceland’s Women’s Day Off on 24 October 1975 saw women leave paid and domestic work and helped accelerate the country’s push for equality.
Delano grape boycott — The Delano grape strike and consumer boycott began in 1965 and helped farmworkers win contracts from California growers.
Bristol Bus Boycott — The Bristol Bus Boycott challenged the Bristol Omnibus Company’s discriminatory employment policy and helped build momentum for Britain’s Race Relations Act 1965.
1968 Olympics Black Power salute — The 1968 Olympic podium salute by Smith and Carlos protested racial inequality and became an enduring image of the Black Power and human-rights movements.
Rumble in the Jungle — The Rumble in the Jungle was the 1974 Ali–Foreman bout in Kinshasa, promoted internationally while Mobutu used it to display Zaire.
Football War — The 1969 Football War grew from deeper political and social tensions between Honduras and El Salvador, although football matches helped trigger the immediate crisis.
Blood in the Water match — The Blood in the Water match was Hungary’s violent 1956 Olympic water-polo victory over the Soviet Union, played against the background of the crushed Hungarian Revolution.
1981 Springbok tour protests — The 1981 Springbok tour triggered months of large and sometimes violent protests across New Zealand over rugby links with apartheid South Africa.

supportingSource.title: 1981 South Africa rugby union tour of New Zealand and the United States

assertion: Nuremberg trials — The Nuremberg trials began with the International Military Tribunal of major Nazi leaders and helped establish individual responsibility for international crimes.
Eichmann trial — Adolf Eichmann’s 1961 trial in Jerusalem publicised survivor testimony and ended in his conviction for crimes against humanity and the Jewish people.
Scopes Monkey Trial — The Scopes Monkey Trial tested Tennessee’s Butler Act after teacher John T. Scopes agreed to be charged with teaching evolution.
McLibel case — In McLibel, McDonald’s pursued Helen Steel and David Morris for libel, generating years of publicity and a later European human-rights judgment.
Rivonia Trial — The 1963–64 Rivonia Trial ended with Mandela and seven co-defendants receiving life sentences.
U-2 incident — The U-2 incident derailed the Paris summit after Powers survived the shoot-down and the Soviet Union revealed his reconnaissance mission.
Stanislav Petrov incident — In the Stanislav Petrov incident, the officer treated satellite warnings as a likely malfunction; later investigation confirmed a false alarm.
Acoustic Kitty — Acoustic Kitty was a 1960s CIA attempt to use a surgically modified cat as a mobile eavesdropping device; the project was abandoned.
Able Archer 83 — Able Archer 83 simulated NATO nuclear procedures; Soviet reactions later made it a central episode in discussion of the 1983 war scare.
Operation Gold — Operation Gold was the CIA and SIS tunnel operation that intercepted Soviet military communications until its carefully timed public discovery in 1956.
Bella ciao — Bella ciao became associated with the Italian resistance and has since travelled worldwide as a protest song, with Money Heist renewing its popularity.
Wind of Change — Wind of Change was inspired by the Scorpions’ Soviet experiences and became widely associated with the fall of the Iron Curtain.
99 Luftballons — The German original 99 Luftballons turns harmless balloons into a chain of military reactions and devastation; its separately written English version is titled 99 Red Balloons.
Free Nelson Mandela — Free Nelson Mandela was written by Dammers and recorded by the Special A.K.A.; it became a prominent musical call for Mandela’s release.
Beds Are Burning — Beds Are Burning was Midnight Oil’s 1987 political song about returning land to the Pintupi people and became a chart hit in several countries.
Britannia — Britannia is the female national personification of Britain, conventionally shown with helmet, trident, and shield.
Russian Bear — The Russian Bear is a widespread visual personification of Russia, originating in Western European imagery and later used inside Russia as well.
Marianne — Marianne is the national personification of the French Republic and is commonly shown wearing the liberty-associated Phrygian cap.
John Bull — John Bull is a male national personification of Britain, developed from a literary character and made familiar through cartoons.
Johnny Canuck — Johnny Canuck began as a Canadian political-cartoon figure and was reinvented in 1942 to fight Nazism; the Vancouver Canucks later used his image as a team logo.

assertion: Bay of Pigs invasion — The Bay of Pigs invasion was an unsuccessful US-backed landing by Cuban exiles against Castro’s government in April 1961.
Potsdam Conference — The 1945 Potsdam Conference brought together the United States, Soviet Union, and United Kingdom to administer defeated Germany and settle post-war questions.
Bandung Conference — The Bandung Conference gathered newly independent and decolonising states and helped lay foundations for the Non-Aligned Movement.
Battle of Seattle — The Battle of Seattle refers to the large demonstrations and direct action around the WTO Ministerial Conference in Seattle in late 1999.
Sharpeville massacre — The Sharpeville massacre became a turning point in resistance to apartheid and prompted a state of emergency and bans on opposition organisations.
Emperor Palpatine — Emperor Palpatine, also known as Darth Sidious, engineers the fall of the Republic and rules the Galactic Empire in Star Wars.
President Snow — President Coriolanus Snow is Panem’s authoritarian ruler and Katniss Everdeen’s chief political enemy in The Hunger Games.
Napoleon the pig — Napoleon the pig seizes power after the rebellion in Animal Farm, expels Snowball, and develops into a dictator.
Frank Underwood — Frank Underwood is the central political operator of the US House of Cards, rising from House Majority Whip to president and repeatedly breaking the fourth wall.
Malcolm Tucker — Malcolm Tucker is Peter Capaldi’s famously profane Director of Communications and political enforcer in The Thick of It.
2016 Brexit referendum — The 2016 Brexit referendum produced a Leave majority and set the United Kingdom on the path to withdrawing from the EU.

supportingSource.title: 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum

assertion: 2014 Scottish independence referendum — The 2014 Scottish independence referendum kept Scotland in the United Kingdom after 55.3 percent voted No.
1995 Quebec referendum — The 1995 Quebec referendum rejected sovereignty by 50.58 percent to 49.42 percent, one of Canada’s closest major votes.
1992 South African apartheid referendum — The 1992 South African apartheid referendum gave de Klerk a mandate from the white electorate to continue negotiations toward ending minority rule.
1999 Australian republic referendum — The 1999 Australian republic referendum rejected the proposed parliamentary-republic model and retained the constitutional monarchy.
Rudolf Nureyev — Rudolf Nureyev defected in Paris in 1961 and became one of the twentieth century’s most celebrated ballet dancers in the West.
Kim Philby — Kim Philby spied for the Soviet Union while serving British intelligence and escaped from Beirut to Moscow when suspicion closed in.
Svetlana Alliluyeva — Svetlana Alliluyeva, Joseph Stalin’s only daughter, defected via the US embassy in New Delhi, settled in the United States, and later used the name Lana Peters.
Viktor Belenko — Viktor Belenko defected by flying his MiG-25 to Japan; the aircraft was dismantled for examination and later returned to the Soviet Union.
Oleg Gordievsky — Oleg Gordievsky was a senior KGB officer and British double agent whose SIS extraction concealed him in a car boot and carried him across the Soviet–Finnish border.
German reunification — German reunification brought East and West Germany together in 1990, with the eastern states acceding to the Federal Republic.
Velvet Divorce — The Velvet Divorce was the negotiated and nonviolent dissolution of Czechoslovakia into two independent states.
Macau handover — The Macau handover transferred sovereignty from Portugal to China and established Macau as a Chinese special administrative region.
Singapore's separation from Malaysia — Singapore's separation from Malaysia in 1965 made it an independent state after a short and troubled period inside the Malaysian federation.
Yemeni unification — Yemeni unification joined North Yemen and South Yemen on 22 May 1990 to create the Republic of Yemen.
Cod Wars — The Cod Wars were the Iceland–United Kingdom disputes over fishing rights that ended with Iceland securing a 200-nautical-mile zone.
Whisky War — The Whisky War was the peaceful Canadian–Danish sovereignty dispute over Hans Island, marked by exchanged flags, notes, and bottles until a 2022 border agreement.
Pig War — The Pig War was a bloodless United States–British confrontation over the San Juan Islands, triggered when Lyman Cutlar shot a pig.
Pastry War — The Pastry War was France’s first intervention in Mexico, named for a pastry cook’s damages claim among wider French demands.
War of the Stray Dog — The War of the Stray Dog, also called the Incident at Petrich, was a brief Greek–Bulgarian crisis halted through League of Nations intervention.
1991 Soviet coup attempt — The 1991 Soviet coup attempt, also called the August Coup, collapsed within days and accelerated the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
2016 Turkish coup attempt — The 2016 Turkish coup attempt was launched by a military faction and collapsed after violent clashes and mass public resistance.
Kapp Putsch — The Kapp Putsch challenged the Weimar Republic under Wolfgang Kapp and Walther von Lüttwitz and failed when workers paralysed the country.
1981 Spanish coup attempt — The 1981 Spanish coup attempt, commonly called 23-F, failed after the seizure of parliament did not win the king or the wider military.
Algiers putsch — The Algiers putsch was a short-lived military revolt by generals who wanted to keep French Algeria and opposed de Gaulle’s policy.
Charlie Hebdo — Charlie Hebdo is a French satirical newspaper whose cartoons and strongly secular editorial stance have repeatedly provoked controversy.
The Daily Show — The Daily Show is a US satirical news programme whose mock newscast format made Jon Stewart a prominent political-comedy figure.
The Colbert Report — The Colbert Report used Colbert’s fictional pundit persona to parody personality-driven US cable news from 2005 to 2014.

Private Eye — Private Eye combines satirical cartoons and recurring jokes with investigations into politics, business, and the press.
BBC Dad — BBC Dad was the moniker Robert Kelly acquired after the family interruption of his 2017 live television interview became a worldwide hit.

Ceaușescu's final speech — Ceaușescu's final speech on 21 December 1989 exposed the regime’s loss of control when a supposedly loyal crowd turned against him on live television.
Walter Cronkite — Walter Cronkite’s 1968 Vietnam special concluded that negotiation, rather than claims of victory, was the only rational way out of the war.
See It Now — See It Now aired the influential McCarthy report in March 1954 and answered the senator in a later episode after CBS offered him reply time.

supportingSource.title: Edward R. Murrow aired historic Joseph McCarthy report 63 years ago today

assertion: Arnold Schwarzenegger — Arnold Schwarzenegger moved from bodybuilding and the Terminator films into politics, serving as governor of California after the 2003 recall election.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy — Volodymyr Zelenskyy built a career in comedy and acting, portrayed a fictional president in Servant of the People, and then won Ukraine’s 2019 presidential election.
Ronald Reagan — Ronald Reagan worked as a film actor and Screen Actors Guild president, served as California governor, and later became US president.
Imran Khan — Imran Khan captained Pakistan’s World Cup-winning cricket team, founded Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, and became prime minister in 2018.
George Weah — George Weah won the 1995 Ballon d’Or after starring in European football and was elected president of Liberia in 2017.
Kennedy family — The Kennedy family produced President John F. Kennedy and prominent politicians Robert and Ted Kennedy.
Bush family — The Bush family includes presidents George H. W. and George W. Bush and former Florida governor Jeb Bush.
Trudeau family — The Trudeau family produced Canadian prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and his son Justin Trudeau.
Nehru–Gandhi family — The Nehru–Gandhi family links Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, and Rajiv Gandhi, all prime ministers of India; Mahatma Gandhi was not a member.
Bhutto family — The Bhutto family includes Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and his daughter Benazir Bhutto, both prime ministers of Pakistan.
Borat — Borat is the 2006 mockumentary built around Cohen’s invented reporter; Kazakhstan’s government denounced its portrayal and the film faced bans in several countries.
The Great Dictator — The Great Dictator was Chaplin’s 1940 anti-fascist satire, in which he played both a Jewish barber and the dictator Adenoid Hynkel.
The Interview — The Interview is a Rogen–Franco comedy about an assassination plot against Kim Jong-un; threats and the Sony cyberattack disrupted its planned theatrical release.
The Death of Stalin — The Death of Stalin satirises the Soviet leadership struggle after Stalin died and was effectively banned from Russian cinemas in 2018.
The Battle of Algiers — The Battle of Algiers dramatises the 1950s urban conflict between the FLN and French authorities in Algiers using a documentary-like visual style.
Edward VIII — Edward VIII abdicated after less than a year as king because the government opposed his planned marriage to the divorced American Wallis Simpson.
Pope Benedict XVI — Pope Benedict XVI, born Joseph Ratzinger, resigned in 2013 and became pope emeritus.
Boris Yeltsin — Boris Yeltsin resigned on 31 December 1999, apologised for unfulfilled hopes, and transferred presidential duties to Putin.
Jacinda Ardern — Jacinda Ardern announced her resignation in January 2023, explaining that she no longer had the energy needed for the role.
Shinzo Abe — Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister, resigned in 2020 because ulcerative colitis had returned.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva — Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, widely called Lula, returned from imprisonment and legal disqualification to win a third presidential term in Brazil.
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan — Recep Tayyip Erdoğan served prison time over a public poetry recital before leading the AKP, governing as prime minister, and becoming president of Turkey.
José Mujica — José “Pepe” Mujica was imprisoned during Uruguay’s military era and later served as president from 2010 to 2015.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf — Ellen Johnson Sirleaf survived imprisonment and exile, won Liberia’s presidency, and received the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize.
Kim Dae-jung — Kim Dae-jung endured kidnapping, prison, and a death sentence before becoming South Korea’s president and winning the 2000 Nobel Peace Prize.

Marie Antoinette said “Let them eat cake” — There is no reliable evidence that Marie Antoinette said “Let them eat cake”; a similar brioche line appeared earlier in Rousseau’s Confessions.
Nero fiddled while Rome burned — The image of Nero fiddling while Rome burned is a later legend; some ancient accounts instead mention singing or a lyre, and the violin was anachronistic.
Mussolini made the trains run on time — The claim that Mussolini made Italian trains run on time was propaganda: earlier governments had made many improvements, and punctuality remained uneven.

assertion: King Canute believed he could stop the tide — Canute staged the command to demonstrate that he could not control nature; the misconception reverses the lesson and portrays him as believing the tide would obey.
Malala Yousafzai — Malala Yousafzai received the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize for defending children’s right to education and became the youngest Nobel winner.

International Committee of the Red Cross — The International Committee of the Red Cross is the only organization to have received the Nobel Peace Prize three times, including the centenary award shared in 1963.

supportingSource.title: International Committee of the Red Cross

assertion: Aung San Suu Kyi — Aung San Suu Kyi received the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize while detained in Myanmar; her sons represented her at the ceremony.

International Campaign to Ban Landmines — The International Campaign to Ban Landmines and Jody Williams received the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize for their work toward banning and clearing anti-personnel mines.
Lê Đức Thọ — Lê Đức Thọ refused the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize because, despite the Paris Peace Accords, peace had not actually been established in Vietnam.
Europe Day — Europe Day on 9 May commemorates the Schuman Declaration, regarded as a founding step toward today’s European Union.
Juneteenth — Juneteenth commemorates the enforcement of emancipation in Texas on 19 June 1865 and is now a US federal holiday.
ANZAC Day — ANZAC Day began as a commemoration of Australian and New Zealand soldiers at Gallipoli and now honours their wider military service and sacrifice.
Day of Reconciliation — The Day of Reconciliation was created in 1995 to acknowledge different South African histories and promote unity after apartheid.
Waitangi Day — Waitangi Day commemorates the first signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, a foundational and contested document in New Zealand history.
The Communist Manifesto — The Communist Manifesto set out a concise account of class struggle and called on workers of all countries to unite.
The Little Red Book — The Little Red Book is the popular name for Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung, one of the most widely printed political books in history.
Letter from Birmingham Jail — Letter from Birmingham Jail argues that people have a moral responsibility to resist unjust laws and explains why waiting for civil rights was unacceptable.
Common Sense — Common Sense attacked monarchy and argued for American independence in language intended for a broad colonial audience.
The Green Book — The Green Book outlined Gaddafi’s claimed alternative to capitalism and communism and became compulsory ideological reading in his Libya.
Iron Lady — “Iron Lady” was the Soviet-coined nickname that became inseparable from Margaret Thatcher’s uncompromising public image.
Madiba — “Madiba,” Mandela’s Thembu clan name, became a widely used respectful form of address for him.
Uncle Ho — Ho Chi Minh was widely known by the affectionate political nickname “Uncle Ho.”
El Comandante — Fidel Castro was widely called “El Comandante,” a title rooted in his leadership of the Cuban Revolution.
Great Helmsman — Mao Zedong was celebrated in official political culture as the “Great Helmsman,” casting him as the guide steering China.
MeToo movement — The MeToo movement grew from Burke’s activism into a global wave of survivor testimony amplified by the #MeToo hashtag.
Kony 2012 — Kony 2012 was Invisible Children’s viral campaign to make Joseph Kony internationally famous and press for his capture.
Bring Back Our Girls — Bring Back Our Girls used the #BringBackOurGirls hashtag to demand the return of the abducted Chibok schoolgirls.
SOPA/PIPA blackout — The SOPA/PIPA blackout was the January 2012 web protest against the Stop Online Piracy Act and PROTECT IP Act.
It Gets Better Project — The It Gets Better Project collected encouraging videos intended to show bullied LGBT young people that life can improve.
Larry — Larry is the resident Downing Street cat whose formal job title is Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office.
Bo — Bo was the Obama family’s Portuguese Water Dog and one of the best-known White House pets of the 2010s.
Socks — Socks was the Clinton family’s adopted stray and became a highly visible White House cat during Bill Clinton’s presidency.
Pushinka — Pushinka was Strelka’s puppy, sent by Nikita Khrushchev to the Kennedy family during the Cold War.
Checkers — Checkers was the dog Nixon named in his successful televised defence against allegations about campaign funds.
British window tax — The British window tax tied the bill to the number of windows, leaving blocked openings as a visible architectural legacy.
Russian beard tax — Peter the Great’s Russian beard tax made payers carry a token proving they had paid to retain their beards.
Vespasian’s urine tax — Vespasian’s urine tax applied to trade in urine collected from public urinals; the episode is linked to the phrase pecunia non olet, “money does not stink.”
British hat tax — The British hat tax was collected through licences and revenue stamps fixed inside hats, with penalties for forgery.
Mussolini’s bachelor tax — Mussolini’s bachelor tax charged unmarried Italian men as part of the regime’s demographic campaign.
Wellington boot — The Wellington boot developed from footwear commissioned by the Duke of Wellington and later became the familiar waterproof “wellie.”
Nehru jacket — The Nehru jacket is a fitted, hip-length coat with a mandarin collar named after Jawaharlal Nehru.
Churchill cigar — Churchill visited Romeo y Julieta in Havana in 1946, and its seven-inch Julieta No. 2 size became known as a Churchill cigar.
Bismarck herring — Bismarck herring is a named form of pickled herring; the response requires both the political surname and the food.
Eisenhower jacket — The Eisenhower jacket, also called the Ike jacket, was the short wool field jacket associated with General Dwight D. Eisenhower and later made standard issue.
Principality of Sealand — The Principality of Sealand is the micronation Bates proclaimed on Fort Roughs off the English coast.
Republic of Užupis — The Republic of Užupis is Vilnius’s bohemian neighbourhood republic, proclaimed on 1 April with a deliberately whimsical constitution.
Liberland — Liberland is Jedlička’s claimed micronation on the Danube borderland between Croatia and Serbia.
Rose Island — Rose Island was Rosa’s artificial-platform micronation off the Italian coast, later dramatized in a Netflix film of the same name.
Conch Republic — The Conch Republic was Key West’s tongue-in-cheek 1982 secession protest against the Border Patrol checkpoint.
Ceylon — Sri Lanka gained independence as the Dominion of Ceylon, retained Ceylon as its country name, and adopted Sri Lanka on becoming a republic in 1972.
Persia — Persia was the long-established Western exonym for Iran; the 1935 request concerned international usage, not the legal creation of a new state.
Siam — Siam was the internationally familiar name of the country officially renamed Thailand in 1939.
Zaire — Zaire was the Mobutu-era name of the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo; Kabila restored a Congo-based name in 1997.
Upper Volta — The Republic of Upper Volta became Burkina Faso under Sankara; its former name referred to the upper Volta River basin.
